nodes.label: Regulatory Requirements, IP and Global Market Success
nodes.summary: Co-editors' introduction to Part 2, covering the nontechnical knowledge needed for global product success: changing regulations, market access by region, and patenting. Highlights ICCR harmonization topics, especially alternatives to animal testing and nanomaterials.

nodes.label: Regulatory Harmonization
nodes.summary: Alignment of cosmetic regulations across countries; harmonized guidelines streamline assessment, reduce development time and duplication, and minimize in vivo testing without compromising safety.

nodes.label: International Cooperation on Cosmetics Regulation
nodes.summary: International group of cosmetic regulators from Canada, the EU, Japan and the US promoting regulatory convergence; its topics include animal testing alternatives, in silico models, nanomaterials, trace impurities, endocrine disruptors and allergens.

nodes.label: Animal Testing
nodes.summary: Historical basis of chemical safety testing; being phased out for cosmetics under consumer pressure and regulatory recognition of its lack of humaneness, the highest-priority regulatory topic.

nodes.label: Alternatives to Animal Testing
nodes.summary: Human-relevant non-animal methods (predictive models, in vitro tests, pathway-based toxicity information) increasingly used for cosmetic safety assessment.

nodes.label: In Silico Prediction Models
nodes.summary: Computer prediction models for safety assessment, an ICCR discussion topic.

nodes.label: Nanomaterials
nodes.summary: Under EU Regulation 1223/2009, insoluble or biopersistent, intentionally manufactured materials with one or more external dimensions or internal structure on the 1-100 nm scale; subject of evolving global legislation.

nodes.label: Trace Impurities
nodes.summary: Unintended trace contaminants in cosmetic ingredients or products; an ICCR priority topic and a focus of safety assessment.

nodes.label: Endocrine Disruptors
nodes.summary: Substances interfering with hormone systems; listed as a key ICCR regulatory topic.

nodes.label: Allergens
nodes.summary: Sensitizing substances, notably fragrance components; an ICCR regulatory topic and subject of EU labeling thresholds.

nodes.label: European Union
nodes.summary: Phased out animal testing for cosmetics, culminating in a 2013 marketing ban on animal-tested products; its Regulation 1223/2009 governs cosmetics.

nodes.label: China
nodes.summary: Major market where imported cosmetics require CFDA registration and animal testing; announced removal of mandatory animal tests for domestic non-special-use cosmetics from June 2014.

nodes.label: China Food and Drug Administration
nodes.summary: Chinese authority (formerly SFDA) regulating cosmetics since taking over from the Ministry of Health in 2008; requires registration and animal testing for imported cosmetics.

nodes.label: EU Animal Testing Ban for Cosmetics
nodes.summary: EU prohibition (Art. 18 of Regulation 1223/2009) on animal testing of cosmetic products and ingredients and on marketing animal-tested products, fully applicable from March 2013.

nodes.label: EU Cosmetics Regulation 1223/2009
nodes.summary: EU cosmetics law applicable since July 11, 2013, replacing Directive 76/768/EEC; requires CPNP notification, a Responsible Person, a Product Information File with safety report, GMP per ISO 22716, and defines nanomaterials.

nodes.label: Food and Drug Administration
nodes.summary: US agency overseeing cosmetics under the FD&C Act; provides compliance guidelines, monitors the market, inspects facilities, but requires no premarket approval or registration for cosmetics.

nodes.label: FDA Draft Guidance on Safety of Nanomaterials in Cosmetic Products
nodes.summary: 2012 FDA draft guidance noting nanomaterials may affect safety and effectiveness; FDA has no formal definition but refers to materials of roughly 1-100 nm, and recommends tailored testing.

nodes.label: Nanotechnology
nodes.summary: Intentional manipulation, manufacture or selection of materials with at least one dimension of about 1-100 nm; a rapidly expanding field driving new legislation.

nodes.label: Social Media Influence on Regulation
nodes.summary: Rapid online spread of information on bad practices or emerging issues accelerates regulatory change and can force removal of ingredients.

nodes.label: Non-Special-Use Cosmetics (China)
nodes.summary: Chinese category including hair care, nail care, skin care, perfumes and makeup; domestically made ones exempt from animal tests from June 2014.

nodes.label: Special-Use Cosmetics (China)
nodes.summary: Chinese category of higher-risk cosmetics: hair growth, hair dye, perm, hair removal, breast shaping, fitness, deodorizing, spot removal and sun block; require registration.

nodes.label: Changing Regulatory Landscape in the U.S. and E.U.
nodes.summary: Overview of US (FD&C Act, FPLA) and EU (Regulation 1223/2009) cosmetic regulation: definitions, classification, labeling, INCI, safety assessment, GMP, PIF/CPSR, CPNP notification, RAPEX and REACH. Concludes that simultaneous compliance is possible since EU compliance largely satisfies US guidelines.

nodes.label: United States
nodes.summary: Market where cosmetic law (since 1938) rests on the responsibility of the firm placing products on the market, with postmarket verification rather than premarket approval.

nodes.label: Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act
nodes.summary: Main US law for cosmetics (adopted 1938); defines cosmetics (excluding soap) and drugs, and prohibits adulterated (Sec. 601) and misbranded (Sec. 602) cosmetics.

nodes.label: Fair Packaging and Labeling Act
nodes.summary: US law that, with the FD&C Act, regulates cosmetic labeling so packages give correct content information and allow comparison.

nodes.label: Adulterated Cosmetic
nodes.summary: Under FD&C Act Sec. 601, a cosmetic containing poisonous/deleterious or filthy substances, prepared under insanitary conditions, in a harmful container, or with an unsafe color additive (hair dyes excepted).

nodes.label: Misbranded Cosmetic
nodes.summary: Under FD&C Act Sec. 602, a cosmetic with false or misleading labeling, missing or inconspicuous required information, or a misleading container.

nodes.label: Legal Definition of Cosmetic
nodes.summary: US: articles applied to the body for cleansing, beautifying, promoting attractiveness or altering appearance (excluding soap). EU: substances placed on external body parts, teeth or oral mucosa exclusively or mainly to clean, perfume, change appearance, protect, keep in good condition or correct odours.

nodes.label: Cosmetic/Drug Combination Product
nodes.summary: US category for products with both cosmetic and drug function (e.g., anti-dandruff shampoo, antiperspirant-deodorant, fluoride toothpaste, SPF moisturizers); must meet both requirements; not allowed in the EU.

nodes.label: Cosmeceuticals
nodes.summary: Marketing term not recognized by the FDA (nor by China); a product with significant physiological action is a drug or cosmetic/drug.

nodes.label: Intended Use Doctrine
nodes.summary: In the US, cosmetic vs drug classification depends on intended use determined by labeling/advertising claims, consumer perception and ingredients, not only composition.

nodes.label: Drug Claims
nodes.summary: Claims the FDA regards as making a product a drug: hair growth restoration, cellulite reduction, varicose vein treatment, skin whitening or darkening, cell regeneration.

nodes.label: New Drug Application
nodes.summary: FDA premarket approval route (FD&C Act sec. 505) required for drugs unless they comply with an OTC monograph.

nodes.label: OTC Drug Monographs
nodes.summary: Standards from FDA's Over-the-Counter Drug Review; cosmetic/drugs must comply and use 'Drug Facts' labeling (21 CFR 201.66) listing active then inactive ingredients.

nodes.label: Good Manufacturing Practice
nodes.summary: Manufacturing quality rules; mandatory for US drugs (21 CFR 210/211) but only guidelines for US cosmetics; mandatory in EU via ISO 22716 (Art. 8).

nodes.label: Voluntary Cosmetic Registration Program
nodes.summary: FDA's voluntary database where firms may register cosmetic products on the US market; registration is not mandatory.

nodes.label: Drug Registration and Listing System
nodes.summary: Mandatory FDA registration for drugs (FD&C Act sec. 510, 21 CFR 207), unlike cosmetics.

nodes.label: Soap
nodes.summary: In the US, a product whose nonvolatile matter is mainly alkali salts of fatty acids and sold solely as soap; regulated by CPSC, not FDA, unless it has cosmetic claims or ingredients. Classified as cosmetic in the EU.

nodes.label: Consumer Product Safety Commission
nodes.summary: US agency that regulates true soaps instead of the FDA.

nodes.label: Principal Display Panel
nodes.summary: Part of the US label seen at retail; must carry product name, identity, warnings where applicable and net quantity in the bottom 30%.

nodes.label: Cosmetic Labeling Requirements
nodes.summary: Rules on label content: US PDP and information panels with letter size rules; EU name/address of RP, nominal content, minimum durability or PAO, precautions, batch number, function and ingredient list.

nodes.label: Mandatory Cosmetic Warning Statements
nodes.summary: US warnings required for unsubstantiated safety (21 CFR 740.10), aerosols, feminine deodorant sprays and foaming detergent bath products.

nodes.label: Ingredient Declaration
nodes.summary: Ingredients listed in descending order of predominance; those at 1% or below and colorants may follow in any order; US trade-secret ingredients may be listed as 'and other ingredients'.

nodes.label: International Nomenclature of Cosmetic Ingredients
nodes.summary: Conventional worldwide naming system for cosmetic ingredient labeling; presence of an INCI name does not authorize an ingredient, nor does absence prohibit it.

nodes.label: International Cosmetic Ingredient Dictionary
nodes.summary: PCPC (former CTFA) publication of INCI names; updated every two years until 2010, online as wINCI from 2011; new names requested online via INCI application.

nodes.label: Personal Care Products Council
nodes.summary: US industry association (formerly CTFA) that manages, publishes and assigns INCI names.

nodes.label: Trade Secret Ingredient Exemption
nodes.summary: FDA may accept an ingredient as a trade secret (21 CFR 720.8) so its name need not be disclosed on the label.

nodes.label: FDA Prohibited Cosmetic Ingredients
nodes.summary: Short FDA list (about 8 substances) banned in cosmetics: bithionol, CFC propellants, chloroform, halogenated salicylanilides, methylene chloride, vinyl chloride, zirconium complexes in aerosols, prohibited cattle materials.

nodes.label: Bithionol
nodes.summary: Prohibited in US cosmetics due to photocontact sensitization (21 CFR 700.11).

nodes.label: Chlorofluorocarbon Propellants
nodes.summary: Prohibited in US cosmetics (21 CFR 700.23).

nodes.label: Chloroform
nodes.summary: Prohibited in US cosmetics based on animal carcinogenicity (21 CFR 700.18).

nodes.label: Halogenated Salicylanilides
nodes.summary: Di-, tri-, metabromsalan and tetrachlorosalicylanilide; prohibited in US cosmetics due to photocontact sensitization (21 CFR 700.15).

nodes.label: Methylene Chloride
nodes.summary: Prohibited in US cosmetics due to animal carcinogenicity (21 CFR 700.19).

nodes.label: Vinyl Chloride
nodes.summary: Prohibited in US cosmetics due to carcinogenicity (21 CFR 700.14).

nodes.label: Zirconium-Containing Complexes
nodes.summary: Prohibited in US aerosol cosmetics because of toxic lung effects including granuloma formation (21 CFR 700.16).

nodes.label: Prohibited Cattle Materials
nodes.summary: Banned in US cosmetics to protect against BSE; excludes tallow with at most 0.15% insoluble impurities, tallow derivatives, hides and milk products.

nodes.label: Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy
nodes.summary: 'Mad cow disease'; reason for US ban on prohibited cattle materials and Chinese BSE certificate requirement.

nodes.label: Photocontact Sensitization
nodes.summary: Light-induced skin sensitization; basis for the US ban on bithionol and halogenated salicylanilides.

nodes.label: Granuloma
nodes.summary: Lung lesion formation caused by zirconium complexes in aerosol cosmetics.

nodes.label: Hexachlorophene
nodes.summary: Restricted US preservative: only when no equally effective alternative, max 0.1%, not on mucous membranes such as lips (21 CFR 250.250).

nodes.label: Mercury Compounds
nodes.summary: Restricted in US: eye-area cosmetics below 65 ppm Hg (about 100 ppm phenylmercuric acetate/nitrate) only if no other preservative works; other cosmetics below 1 ppm unavoidable trace.

nodes.label: Preservatives
nodes.summary: Ingredients ensuring self-preservation of water-containing cosmetics used in nonsterile conditions; EU positive list in Annex V, free in US.

nodes.label: Sunscreen
nodes.summary: Classified as a drug in the US (sunscreen ingredients used only for product color protection must be qualified) but as a cosmetic in the EU.

nodes.label: UV Filters
nodes.summary: Sunscreen actives; EU positive list in Annex VI, allowed only in drugs in the US.

nodes.label: Color Additives
nodes.summary: Dyes regulated by positive list in US (21 CFR 73/74, FDA approval; batch-certified or exempt) and EU (Annex IV, identified by colour index).

nodes.label: Coal-Tar Dyes (Certified Colors)
nodes.summary: Petroleum-derived color additives that must be FDA batch-certified because of possible contamination, e.g. FD&C Red No. 40, FD&C Yellow No. 5.

nodes.label: Certification-Exempt Color Additives
nodes.summary: Colorants from mineral, plant or animal sources exempt from FDA batch certification, e.g. iron oxides, titanium dioxide, mica, carmine, zinc oxide.

nodes.label: Titanium Dioxide
nodes.summary: Certification-exempt color additive (21 CFR 73.2575); nano TiO2 widely used in sunscreens and studied for size-dependent lung inflammation.

nodes.label: Zinc Oxide
nodes.summary: Certification-exempt color additive (21 CFR 73.2991); restricted in KSA below 25% unless for a medical condition (then a drug).

nodes.label: Iron Oxides
nodes.summary: Certification-exempt color additive (21 CFR 73.2250).

nodes.label: Mica
nodes.summary: Certification-exempt color additive (21 CFR 73.2496).

nodes.label: Carmine
nodes.summary: Certification-exempt color additive of animal origin (21 CFR 73.2087).

nodes.label: Dihydroxyacetone
nodes.summary: Certification-exempt color additive (21 CFR 73.2150).

nodes.label: Lead
nodes.summary: Heavy-metal impurity detected by FDA in some makeup; CU limit 5.0 mg/kg in products with over 1% natural raw materials.

nodes.label: Heavy Metals
nodes.summary: Inevitable impurities on EU forbidden lists, allowed only in technically unavoidable, nonhazardous traces.

nodes.label: Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons
nodes.summary: Inevitable impurities listed among EU forbidden substances.

nodes.label: Nitrosamines
nodes.summary: Inevitable impurities among EU forbidden substances, allowed only in technically unavoidable traces.

nodes.label: Cosmetic Safety Assessment
nodes.summary: Evaluation by a qualified expert of ingredient toxicology, exposure and finished-product tests to conclude a product is safe under normal and foreseeable use; voluntary in US (else warning), compulsory in EU PIF.

nodes.label: Cosmetic Ingredient Review
nodes.summary: Independent expert panel meeting quarterly to evaluate cosmetic ingredient safety; its monographs are cited by FDA as information sources.

nodes.label: Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety
nodes.summary: EU Commission scientific committee issuing ingredient safety opinions and 'Notes of Guidance' (incl. MoS calculation and nanomaterial guidance).

nodes.label: SCCS Notes of Guidance
nodes.summary: SCCS guidelines for testing cosmetic ingredients and safety evaluation; define a 4-step risk assessment and MoS calculation.

nodes.label: Patch Test
nodes.summary: Dermatological patch testing on human volunteers or in vitro skin, a usual finished-product safety test.

nodes.label: HET-CAM Test
nodes.summary: In vitro test of mucous membrane irritation used in finished-product safety evaluation.

nodes.label: Preservative Challenge Test
nodes.summary: Test verifying effectiveness of the preservative system; compulsory in EU, not in US.

nodes.label: Microbiological Contamination
nodes.summary: Contamination of cosmetics; common limits 1000 cfu/g total aerobic count, 500 cfu/g for eye-area products.

nodes.label: FDA Plant Inspection Checklist
nodes.summary: FDA checklist covering buildings, equipment, personnel, raw materials, production, lab controls, records, labeling and complaints; overlaps with ISO 22716.

nodes.label: ISO 22716 Cosmetics GMP
nodes.summary: International GMP standard for cosmetics (2007), mandatory under EU Regulation 1223/2009 Art. 8; structure similar to ISO 9001.

nodes.label: ISO 9001
nodes.summary: General quality management system standard; companies certified to it adapt easily to ISO 22716.

nodes.label: EU Cosmetics Directive 76/768/EEC
nodes.summary: 1976 EU directive based on self-responsibility, replaced by Regulation 1223/2009 in July 2013; model for GSO, Chinese and CU rules.

nodes.label: Cosmetic Products Notification Portal
nodes.summary: EU online portal where the Responsible Person must notify products (category, RP, nanomaterials, CMR, frame formulation, label) before market placement; not an authorization.

nodes.label: Product Information File
nodes.summary: Compulsory EU dossier (Art. 11) with product description, CPSR, manufacturing/GMP statement, proof of claimed effects and animal testing data; available to authorities.

nodes.label: Cosmetic Product Safety Report
nodes.summary: Annex I report within the PIF: Part A safety information (composition, stability, microbiology, impurities, exposure, toxicology) and Part B safety assessment with reasoning.

nodes.label: Responsible Person
nodes.summary: Natural or legal EU-established person designated for each cosmetic (Art. 4), responsible for compliance with safety, GMP, PIF, notification, labeling, claims and surveillance (Art. 5).

nodes.label: Safety Assessor
nodes.summary: Qualified expert (Art. 10) who writes the CPSR and supervises scientific/technical compliance; must have relevant EU degree and cosmetic experience.

nodes.label: Annex II Prohibited Substances
nodes.summary: EU list of over 1300 substances prohibited in cosmetics; traces allowed only if technically unavoidable and safe (Art. 17).

nodes.label: Annex III Restricted Substances
nodes.summary: EU list of over 250 substances allowed only with concentration limits, use restrictions and warnings.

nodes.label: EU Positive Lists (Annexes IV-VI)
nodes.summary: Colorants (Annex IV), preservatives (Annex V) and UV filters (Annex VI) usable only if listed.

nodes.label: Period After Opening
nodes.summary: Open-jar symbol with months of use after opening, used for products with minimum durability over 30 months instead of a date.

nodes.label: Fragrance Allergen Labeling
nodes.summary: EU requirement to label 26 allergens (Annex III 67-92) above 0.001% in leave-on and 0.01% in rinse-off products.

nodes.label: Gas Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry
nodes.summary: Multiresidual analysis used to determine allergen content in perfumes and essential oils.

nodes.label: CosIng Database
nodes.summary: European Commission database on cosmetic substances and ingredients, an unofficial updated nomenclature source pending the Glossary.

nodes.label: Margin of Safety
nodes.summary: MoS = NOAEL / SED; per SCCS should exceed 100.

nodes.label: No Observed Adverse Effect Level
nodes.summary: Highest dose without observed adverse effects; basis for MoS but rarely found in literature.

nodes.label: Systemic Exposure Dosage
nodes.summary: Estimated systemic exposure to an ingredient, the denominator in MoS calculation.

nodes.label: Four-Step Risk Assessment
nodes.summary: SCCS approach: hazard identification, dose-response assessment, exposure assessment, risk characterization; steps 3-4 compulsory under 1223/2009.

nodes.label: CMR Substances
nodes.summary: Carcinogenic, mutagenic or reprotoxic substances per Regulation 1272/2008; category 2 banned unless SCCS-approved; 1A/1B banned except strict conditions.
aliases: carcinogenic, mutagenic or toxic for reproduction

nodes.label: CLP Regulation 1272/2008
nodes.summary: EU classification regulation used to define CMR categories for cosmetics.

nodes.label: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development
nodes.summary: Publishes validated test guidelines; OECD-validated alternative tests accepted in EU.

nodes.label: QSAR
nodes.summary: Theoretical structure-activity studies on hazard used as alternative strategy after animal testing restrictions.

nodes.label: RAPEX
nodes.summary: EU rapid alert system for non-food consumer products; Member States report market anomalies published weekly, frequently involving cosmetics.

nodes.label: Cosmetovigilance
nodes.summary: Reporting of serious undesirable effects by the RP to authorities (Art. 23) and market surveillance by Member States (Art. 22).

nodes.label: REACH Regulation
nodes.summary: EU chemicals regulation (Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals); substances over 1 t/year must be registered with ECHA, polymers and natural substances exempt.

nodes.label: European Chemicals Agency
nodes.summary: EU agency where substances over 1 tonne/year must be registered under REACH.

nodes.label: Cosmetics Europe
nodes.summary: European cosmetics industry association (former Colipa) publishing PIF and labeling guidelines.

nodes.label: Simultaneous US-EU Compliance
nodes.summary: Planning product development from the outset to meet both US and EU rules; EU compliance makes US compliance easier.

nodes.label: Global Market Access: Russia
nodes.summary: Q&A overview of Russian and Customs Union cosmetic market access under Technical Regulation TR CU 009/2011 (in force July 1, 2012), which replaced dual State Registration plus GOST R certification with a single document. Compares CU requirements with EU rules and notes Russia's WTO accession.

nodes.label: Russia
nodes.summary: Dynamic cosmetics market with demand growing 5%+ per year (possibly over 15% until 2015); joined WTO in 2012, reducing import duties.

nodes.label: Eurasian Customs Union
nodes.summary: Customs Union of Russia, Belarus and Kazakhstan formed January 1, 2010 with common tariffs and customs code; single economic area from 2012.

nodes.label: TR CU 009/2011 Safety of Perfumery and Cosmetic Products
nodes.summary: CU technical regulation approved 23.09.2011 (Decree 799), in force July 1, 2012; requires either State Registration or Declaration of Conformity, with composition, physicochemical, microbiological, toxicological and clinical parameters.

nodes.label: CU Unified Sanitary-Epidemiological Requirements (Decree 299)
nodes.summary: 2010 CU document (28.05.2010) setting unified hygienic requirements and mandatory State Registration.

nodes.label: CU State Registration
nodes.summary: Conformity document for 13 higher-risk cosmetic categories (e.g. tanning, whitening, children's, hair dyes, nanomaterial products, peelings, fluoride oral care); issued to manufacturer, unlimited validity, valid across the CU.

nodes.label: CU TR Declaration of Conformity
nodes.summary: Conformity document for all other cosmetics; issued to a CU-registered legal entity for a specific contract, limited to one client and contract duration.

nodes.label: GOST R Certification
nodes.summary: Former Russian declaration/certificate of conformity with GOST R mark, second step of pre-2012 dual assessment; valid until July 1, 2014.

nodes.label: EAC Conformity Mark
nodes.summary: EurAsian Conformity mark (Decision 711, 2011) required on CU-certified products instead of GOST R mark; minimum 5 mm.

nodes.label: Rospotrebnadzor
nodes.summary: Russian Federal Service for consumer rights supervision named in 2012 (Decree 989) to apply and verify the Technical Regulation.

nodes.label: Rosaccreditatsia
nodes.summary: Russian Federal Accreditation Service assigned control of Technical Regulation application.

nodes.label: World Trade Organization
nodes.summary: Russia joined in 2012 after 18 years of negotiation, committing to SPS and TBT agreements.

nodes.label: Third-Party Conformity Assessment
nodes.summary: CU requires product testing at CU-accredited laboratories and certification bodies before entering the territory.

nodes.label: Arsenic
nodes.summary: Toxic element limited to 5.0 mg/kg in CU cosmetics containing over 1% natural herbal/mineral raw materials.

nodes.label: Mercury
nodes.summary: Toxic element limited to 1.0 mg/kg in CU cosmetics with over 1% natural raw materials.

nodes.label: Candida albicans
nodes.summary: Microorganism not allowed in 0.1 g (cream) or 0.5 g (mascara) under CU requirements.

nodes.label: Escherichia coli
nodes.summary: Pathogen not allowed in CU cosmetic samples.

nodes.label: Staphylococcus aureus
nodes.summary: Pathogen not allowed in CU cosmetic samples.

nodes.label: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
nodes.summary: Pathogen not allowed in CU cosmetic samples.

nodes.label: pH Value
nodes.summary: Physicochemical parameter specified by CU per category: facial/body cream 5.0-9.0, liquid mascara 5.5-8.5; 33 pH categories.

nodes.label: Hydrogen Peroxide
nodes.summary: Dental bleaching agent; products at 0.1-6.0% H2O2 (incl. from carbamide/zinc peroxide) require CU State Registration.

nodes.label: Carbamide Peroxide
nodes.summary: Hydrogen peroxide-releasing dental bleaching ingredient.

nodes.label: Fluoride
nodes.summary: Oral care active; CU State Registration needed above 0.15% (0.05% liquids) and fluoride content labeling required; makes US toothpaste a cosmetic/drug.

nodes.label: Oral Care Products
nodes.summary: Toothpastes and mouthwashes; regulated by separate national standards in China; fluoride products have CU labeling rules.

nodes.label: Mascara
nodes.summary: Eye product; CU limits pH 5.5-8.5 and stricter microbiology (<=10^2 CFU/g).

nodes.label: Facial or Body Cream
nodes.summary: CU limits pH 5.0-9.0 and <=10^3 CFU/g; KSA skin cream standard requires >=15% fatty matter.

nodes.label: Children's Cosmetics
nodes.summary: Higher-risk category requiring CU State Registration and specific labeling; in China subject to 2012 guide minimizing ingredients.

nodes.label: Hair Dyes
nodes.summary: Hair colorants requiring CU State Registration; special-use in China; exempted from some US adulteration rules.

nodes.label: Saudi Arabia Cosmetics Market Access and Regulations
nodes.summary: Overview of cosmetic regulation in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia under the SFDA: sanctioned Gulf standard GSO 1943/2009, SFDA product classification guidance with extra ingredient restrictions, labeling rules (Arabic, country of origin, no medical claims) and shipment-based Certificate of Conformity market access.

nodes.label: Saudi Arabia
nodes.summary: Fast-growing GCC market for cosmetics with strong demand for luxury products, where social customs strongly influence rules.

nodes.label: Gulf Cooperation Council
nodes.summary: Regional bloc of Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, UAE, Qatar, Bahrain and Oman; GSO standards apply across it; also a regional patent organization.

nodes.label: Saudi Food and Drug Authority
nodes.summary: Created 2003, Cosmetic Department since 2008; issues regulations, controls safety, develops standards and runs cosmetovigilance in KSA.

nodes.label: Saudi Arabian Standards Organization
nodes.summary: National standards body that transferred food, drug and cosmetic standards to SFDA in 2011; its standards still apply.

nodes.label: GSO 1943/2009 Cosmetic Products Safety Requirements
nodes.summary: SFDA-sanctioned Gulf standard (equivalent SASO 1953/2009) based on Directive 76/768 with tables of prohibited, restricted substances, colorants, preservatives and UV filters.

nodes.label: SFDA Guidance for Products Classification
nodes.summary: 2012 guideline classifying drugs, herbal, health and cosmetic products; adds bans (tretinoin, hydroquinone, triclosan) and limits (retinol 1%, sulfur 2%, urea 10%, AHAs 10%).

nodes.label: Tretinoin
nodes.summary: Retinoic acid and salts; not permitted at any concentration in KSA cosmetics.

nodes.label: Hydroquinone
nodes.summary: Dihydroxybenzene; prohibited in KSA cosmetics; hydroquinone skin-whitening products excluded from cosmetics.

nodes.label: Triclosan
nodes.summary: Antimicrobial not permitted at any concentration in KSA cosmetics.

nodes.label: Retinol
nodes.summary: Vitamin A; with esters retinyl acetate and palmitate permitted at <=1% in KSA cosmetics.

nodes.label: Retinyl Palmitate
nodes.summary: Retinol ester permitted at <=1% in KSA.

nodes.label: Retinyl Acetate
nodes.summary: Retinol ester permitted at <=1% in KSA.

nodes.label: Sulfur
nodes.summary: Permitted at <=2% in KSA cosmetics.

nodes.label: Urea
nodes.summary: Permitted at <=10% in KSA cosmetics, except bath products to be diluted.

nodes.label: Salicylic Acid
nodes.summary: KSA limits: active <=3% in rinse-off hair products, <=2% elsewhere; preservative <0.5%.

nodes.label: Alpha Hydroxy Acids
nodes.summary: KSA: total <=10% at pH >=3.5; leave-on products >=3% need Arabic/English cautions including sunscreen advice; FDA lists AHAs/BHAs among frequently asked ingredients.

nodes.label: Citric Acid
nodes.summary: May exceed 10% in KSA bath preparations meant to be diluted.

nodes.label: Skin Whitening Products
nodes.summary: Skin lightening cosmetics; hydroquinone-free versions are cosmetics in KSA; require CU State Registration; whitening claims make a US drug.

nodes.label: SASO 1512:2010 Skin Cream Standard
nodes.summary: Product-specific standard (GSO 1152:2010): pH 5-9.5, fatty matter >=15%, water <=85%, utility date <=3 years; used in local lab testing.

nodes.label: SASO 585/2000 Perfumery Products Based on Ethanol
nodes.summary: Requires ethanol denaturation; products with <8% fragrance limited to 250 ml with nonremovable pump and 'for external use only' warning in Arabic.

nodes.label: Perfume
nodes.summary: Fragrance products; ethanol-based perfumes subject to SASO 585/2000 in KSA; fragrances had separate pre-2012 CU assessment.

nodes.label: Ethanol
nodes.summary: Alcohol in perfumery; must be denatured in KSA; alcohol-containing mouthwash banned in KSA since 2011.

nodes.label: Mouthwash
nodes.summary: Alcohol-containing mouthwashes banned by SFDA in 2011 because alcohol-free alternatives exist.

nodes.label: Certificate of Conformity (KSA)
nodes.summary: Required per shipment for cosmetics entering KSA (MoCI Decree 6386), issued by approved inspection bodies after document review, testing and inspection.

nodes.label: Country of Origin Labeling
nodes.summary: Mandatory in KSA (MoCI Royal Decree M/5, 2010); 'Made in EU' or dual-origin wording not accepted.

nodes.label: Arabic Labeling Requirement
nodes.summary: KSA requires at least Arabic for product function, warnings and special instructions.

nodes.label: Global Market Access: China
nodes.summary: Overview of Chinese cosmetic regulation for importers: special vs non-special use categories, CFDA registration documents, mandatory animal testing, impurity-focused safety assessment, comparison with the EU, and the IECIC existing ingredient inventory with slow new-ingredient approval.

nodes.label: Regulations Concerning the Hygiene Supervision over Cosmetics (1990)
nodes.summary: Basis of Chinese cosmetic regulation, defining cosmetics as daily-use chemical products applied to the body surface to clean, deodorize, protect, make up and beautify.

nodes.label: GB 8372-2008 Toothpaste Standard
nodes.summary: Chinese national standard specifying toothpaste requirements; oral care products not in either cosmetic category.

nodes.label: China Cosmetic Product Registration
nodes.summary: CFDA premarket registration required for all imported cosmetics and domestic special-use products, with dossier in simplified Chinese, MOH-accredited lab testing, free sale certificate and BSE certificate; may take months or years.

nodes.label: Guinea Pig Maximization Test
nodes.summary: Animal skin sensitization test (GPMT), prohibited in the EU but the only sensitization method accepted by China FDA.

nodes.label: Local Lymph Node Assay
nodes.summary: Skin sensitization assay (LLNA) recommended under the 3R principle but not accepted by CFDA at the time.

nodes.label: 3R Principle
nodes.summary: Replace, Refine and Reduce animal use in testing.

nodes.label: Skin Sensitization
nodes.summary: Allergic sensitizing potential of products investigated with GPMT or LLNA.

nodes.label: Allergic Contact Dermatitis
nodes.summary: Condition the EU's 26-allergen labeling aims to protect consumers against.

nodes.label: 3T3 Neutral Red Uptake Phototoxicity Test
nodes.summary: First in vitro method approved by CFDA (February 2012), the only accepted in vitro method in China.

nodes.label: Phenol
nodes.summary: Common impurity in phenoxyethanol requiring testing reports in China.

nodes.label: Phenoxyethanol
nodes.summary: Preservative whose common impurity phenol must be tested for Chinese registration.

nodes.label: 1,4-Dioxane
nodes.summary: Routine impurity tested in China with MoS calculation if traces present.

nodes.label: Methanol
nodes.summary: Routine impurity tested in Chinese safety assessment.

nodes.label: Acrylamide
nodes.summary: Routine impurity tested in Chinese safety assessment.

nodes.label: N-Nitrosodiethanolamine
nodes.summary: Nitrosamine impurity (NDELA) routinely tested in China with MoS.

nodes.label: Organic Cosmetics
nodes.summary: Not regulated in the EU; in China organic claims are basically prohibited, third-party certifications not accepted; 95% organic content needed for official 'organic' mark under GB/T 19630.

nodes.label: AQSIQ
nodes.summary: Chinese General Administration of Quality Supervision, Inspection and Quarantine, authority for GB/T 19630 organic products.

nodes.label: Chinese INCI Name
nodes.summary: Chinese labels must list ingredients by Chinese INCI names from the MOH Catalogue of International Cosmetic Ingredients; importers must apply if missing.

nodes.label: Inventory of Existing Cosmetic Ingredients in China
nodes.summary: CFDA inventory (IECIC 2003 & 2011) plus 2012 batches of 1674, 637 and 1356 substances; ingredients outside it are 'new' and need approval.

nodes.label: New Cosmetic Ingredient Registration (China)
nodes.summary: Approval needed before using any ingredient not on the CFDA list; extremely time-consuming; only three approved since 2008.

nodes.label: MAC and MUCAP
nodes.summary: Maximum approved concentration and maximum used concentration in approved products; exceeding MUCAP requires safety evidence.

nodes.label: GB 5296.3-2008 Cosmetic Labeling
nodes.summary: Chinese cosmetic labeling standard; industry applies a Chinese 'patch' over original labels.

nodes.label: Nanomaterials in Cosmetics: Regulatory and Safety
nodes.summary: Reviews regulation of nanomaterial-containing cosmetics in Europe (6-month pre-notification, [nano] labeling, SCCS guidance), the US (FDA draft guidance, no premarket approval) and Canada (notification, hotlist, NSNR under CEPA). Discusses safety assessment issues: study design, physicochemical characterization, dose metrics and assay interference.

nodes.label: EU Nanomaterial Pre-Market Notification
nodes.summary: Products with nanomaterials must be notified six months before market placement with identity, specification, quantity, toxicology, safety data and exposure conditions.

nodes.label: SCCS Guidance on Safety Assessment of Nanomaterials in Cosmetics
nodes.summary: 2012 SCCS guidance listing characterization parameters (size, morphology, surface, solubility, surface area etc.) and recommending characterization in raw, formulated and test states.

nodes.label: [nano] Ingredient Labeling
nodes.summary: EU requirement that nanomaterial ingredients be followed by 'nano' in brackets in the ingredient list.

nodes.label: EU Catalogue of Nanomaterials in Cosmetics
nodes.summary: Public catalogue of nanomaterials used in cosmetics, due by January 11, 2014; nano provisions to be reviewed by July 11, 2018.

nodes.label: Canada
nodes.summary: Market requiring mandatory cosmetic notification to Health Canada; defines nanomaterials as 1-100 nm or exhibiting nanoscale properties.

nodes.label: Health Canada
nodes.summary: Canadian authority receiving Cosmetic Notification Forms, maintaining the ingredient hotlist and issuing 2011 working definition of nanomaterial.

nodes.label: Cosmetic Notification Form
nodes.summary: Must be submitted to Health Canada within ten days of making a cosmetic available, listing ingredients and concentrations.

nodes.label: Cosmetic Ingredient Hotlist
nodes.summary: Health Canada list of prohibited and restricted cosmetic ingredients; no nanomaterials listed as of late 2012.

nodes.label: Canadian Food and Drugs Act
nodes.summary: Canadian law with Cosmetic Regulations; Section 16 allows Health Canada to restrict unsafe ingredients.

nodes.label: Canadian Environmental Protection Act
nodes.summary: CEPA 1999; cosmetic ingredients subject to its New Substances Notification Regulations.

nodes.label: New Substances Notification Regulations
nodes.summary: Volume-based premanufacture/preimport notification under CEPA for substances not on the Domestic Substances List; nanoscale forms with unique structures are new.

nodes.label: Domestic Substances List
nodes.summary: Canadian inventory of existing substances; substances not listed are new under NSNR.

nodes.label: Nanomaterial Physicochemical Characterization
nodes.summary: Characterization of size, distribution, morphology, surface, solubility, purity, agglomeration etc.; paramount for interpreting toxicity; purity lacking in over half of food nanomaterial studies.

nodes.label: Read-Across
nodes.summary: Safety evaluation based on structural surrogates or categories; insufficient data to apply to nanomaterials.

nodes.label: Good Laboratory Practice
nodes.summary: Principles nanomaterial safety studies should ideally follow along with OECD guidelines.

nodes.label: Tiered Testing Strategy
nodes.summary: In vitro and in vivo screening followed by pivotal in vivo and mechanistic studies for nanomaterials.

nodes.label: Dose Metrics for Nanomaterials
nodes.summary: Mass-based doses may be inappropriate for nanomaterials; particle number or surface area may better predict dose-response.

nodes.label: Lung Inflammation
nodes.summary: In rats, 25 nm TiO2 caused steeper inflammation per mass than 250 nm; curves overlapped when dosed by surface area.

nodes.label: Nanomaterial Assay Interference
nodes.summary: Nanomaterials interfere with optical readouts, dyes, ROS measurement and adsorb nutrients/cytokines, causing false positives or negatives.

nodes.label: MTT Assay
nodes.summary: Cell viability assay; carbon nanoparticles adsorb substrate causing false positives; recommended in OECD TG 431 skin corrosion test.

nodes.label: LDH Assay
nodes.summary: Cytotoxicity assay; trace metal nanoparticles inhibit LDH giving false negatives.

nodes.label: ELISA
nodes.summary: Inflammatory cytokine assay; metal oxide nanoparticles adsorb cytokines giving false negatives.

nodes.label: Carbon Nanoparticles
nodes.summary: Adsorb MTT substrate, producing false-positive cytotoxicity.

nodes.label: Metal Oxide Nanoparticles
nodes.summary: Adsorb cytokines in ELISAs, falsely reducing inflammation readouts.

nodes.label: OECD TG 431 In Vitro Skin Corrosion
nodes.summary: Human skin model test using the MTT viability assay, vulnerable to nanomaterial interference.

nodes.label: Reactive Oxygen Species
nodes.summary: Their measurement can be interfered with by nanomaterials.

nodes.label: Nutraceuticals and Beauty from Within
nodes.summary: Growing ingested beauty products; makes toxicology of food-related nanomaterials relevant to cosmetics.

nodes.label: Skin Irritation
nodes.summary: Endpoint FDA recommends evaluating for nanomaterials, along with sensitization, phototoxicity, genotoxicity and repeat-dose toxicity.

nodes.label: Intellectual Property: Patents and Trade Secrets
nodes.summary: Guide to intellectual property for cosmetics: utility, design and plant patents, utility models, patentability criteria, PCT and regional patent systems, trade secrets, trademarks, trade dress and copyright. Also covers freedom to operate, partnering, infringement types, traditional knowledge (TKDL) and patent/trademark searching.

nodes.label: Intellectual Property
nodes.summary: Property right for intangibles allowing owners to profit or exclude others; mainly a license to sue, a barrier to entry in cosmetics.

nodes.label: Patent
nodes.summary: Territorial exclusive right granted for disclosure, generally 20 years from filing; claims define coverage; requires novelty, nonobviousness and utility.

nodes.label: Utility Patent
nodes.summary: Most common patent covering products, processes, product-by-process or new uses (e.g., birch bark extract to reduce wrinkles); 20-year term, about 40% acceptance rate.

nodes.label: U.S. Provisional Patent Application
nodes.summary: Placeholder filed up to 12 months before a regular application to gain term; no direct enforcement value.

nodes.label: Design Patent
nodes.summary: Protects nonfunctional ornamental appearance (e.g., cosmetic bottles, Vaseline jar USD407982); 14-15 years; also called industrial design.

nodes.label: Plant Patent
nodes.summary: For asexually reproduced new plant varieties; 20-year term, single claim, rare.

nodes.label: Utility Model
nodes.summary: 'Patent-lite' in China, Japan, Korea and others; lower inventive step, little examination, about 10 years; not in US.

nodes.label: Novelty
nodes.summary: Patentability condition that the invention was not previously known in the prior art (35 USC 102, EPC Art. 54).

nodes.label: Nonobviousness
nodes.summary: Patentability condition that the invention is not obvious to a person skilled in the art (35 USC 103, EPC Art. 56); hinders broad formulation patents in US.

nodes.label: Industrial Applicability
nodes.summary: Patentability condition of usefulness/operativeness (EPC Art. 57).

nodes.label: First-to-File System
nodes.summary: Since March 16, 2013, US awards patents to the first inventor to file, harmonizing with the rest of the world.

nodes.label: Teaching-Suggestion-Motivation Test
nodes.summary: US obviousness test asking whether prior art suggested combining teachings; makes granted combination patents hard to challenge.

nodes.label: United States Patent and Trademark Office
nodes.summary: US office examining patents and trademarks; PAIR system gives access to file wrappers.

nodes.label: World Intellectual Property Organization
nodes.summary: UN agency dedicated to IP that administers the PCT and Madrid System.

nodes.label: Patent Cooperation Treaty
nodes.summary: WIPO treaty (1970) giving a unified international filing procedure across 146 countries (2012); examination reverts to national offices.

nodes.label: European Patent Convention
nodes.summary: Treaty with EPO offering single application, search and examination for 38 countries (2012); 9-month post-grant opposition.

nodes.label: Unitary Patent and Unified Patent Court
nodes.summary: Planned EU unified patent protection across 25 countries with a common court formed December 2012.

nodes.label: Regional Patent Organizations
nodes.summary: ARIPO (18 mostly English-speaking African states), OAPI (16 French-speaking), EAPO (Eurasian), GCC patent office and Latin American bodies.

nodes.label: Trade Secret Protection
nodes.summary: Protection of secret valuable information (formulas, processes, customer lists) without registration or time limit while kept secret; no protection against independent development or reverse engineering.

nodes.label: Nondisclosure Agreement
nodes.summary: Confidentiality contract (NDA/CDA) protecting trade secrets and confidential information.

nodes.label: Trademark
nodes.summary: Brand distinguishing a company's goods; protected by use and registration, renewable every ten years indefinitely; key test is likelihood of confusion.

nodes.label: Service Mark
nodes.summary: Mark identifying the source of a service rather than a product (e.g., CosmoProf).

nodes.label: Trade Dress
nodes.summary: Limited right in distinctive product appearance or packaging, protected through courts without formal registration.

nodes.label: Copyright
nodes.summary: Protection for original works; in cosmetics covers packaging layouts, slogans, labels and advertising; US term life plus 70 years.

nodes.label: Madrid Protocol
nodes.summary: WIPO system for filing a single trademark application across many countries.

nodes.label: Office for Harmonization in the Internal Market
nodes.summary: EU office organizing European trademarks and designs.

nodes.label: Trademark Class 3
nodes.summary: Nice class covering soaps, perfumery, essential oils, cosmetics, hair lotions and dentifrices; other relevant classes 1, 5, 8, 10, 21, 44.

nodes.label: Berne Convention
nodes.summary: International treaty partly harmonizing copyright protection.

nodes.label: Freedom to Operate Analysis
nodes.summary: Determines whether a product, process or name infringes others' valid IP in target countries; remedies include design-around, invalidation or licensing.

nodes.label: Patent Marking
nodes.summary: Laws require tagging products or packaging (or a website) with protecting patent numbers, revealing IP information.

nodes.label: Patent Infringement
nodes.summary: Unauthorized making, using, selling or importing a patented invention during its term; remedies include injunction and damages.

nodes.label: Direct Infringement
nodes.summary: Most common infringement under 35 USC 271(a).

nodes.label: Indirect Infringement
nodes.summary: Inducement or contributory infringement; requires underlying direct infringement.

nodes.label: Literal Infringement
nodes.summary: Every claim element has identical correspondence in the accused product or process.

nodes.label: Doctrine of Equivalents
nodes.summary: Infringement where an element performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way for the same result.

nodes.label: Willful Infringement
nodes.summary: Intentional copying; courts may award up to triple damages plus attorney fees.

nodes.label: Traditional Knowledge Digital Library
nodes.summary: Indian database documenting traditional medicine knowledge in formats patent examiners understand, preventing misappropriation via patents.

nodes.label: Traditional Herbal Knowledge
nodes.summary: Asian (Indian, Chinese) traditional remedies passed orally; documentation safeguards sovereignty against patenting of nonoriginal innovations.

nodes.label: Patent Classification Systems
nodes.summary: USPC (classes 132, 424, 512, D28), IPC and ECLA (A61K, A61Q) hierarchical classes used for patent searching.

nodes.label: Patent Searching and Mining
nodes.summary: Mining free (Espacenet, PATENTSCOPE, Google Patents) and paid databases for legal and technical competitive intelligence.

nodes.label: File Wrapper (PAIR)
nodes.summary: Collection of application documents and office correspondence retrievable via USPTO PAIR or European Patent Register.

nodes.label: IP in Third-Party Partnering
nodes.summary: Confidentiality and ownership issues in contract R&D, manufacturing, outsourcing and open innovation; file patents before joint projects.

nodes.label: Birch Bark Extract
nodes.summary: Example of a new use patent: using birch bark extract to reduce wrinkles.

nodes.label: Wrinkles
nodes.summary: Skin aging sign; cited as target of patented new-use example.

nodes.label: BB Cream
nodes.summary: Cited example of a new-use patent: BB cream used for hair treatment.

nodes.label: Japan
nodes.summary: ICCR member; Japan Patent Office excludes medical processes, allows post-grant opposition and utility models; deregulated cosmetics in 2001.

nodes.label: India
nodes.summary: Indian patent law excludes cosmetic surgery methods and mere new forms/uses of known substances; has pre- and post-grant opposition; source of TKDL.
